title: Light Wells and Natural Ventilation for Townhouses: Getting It Right
desc: A light well brightens and cools a townhouse, but done wrong it is hot, leaky and noisy. How to choose position and cover, create airflow, and handle safety.
summary: The principles of natural ventilation in a townhouse, how to choose the light well position, cover and railing, and the common mistakes that make a light well hot and leaky.
body: p

A townhouse has neighbours' walls on both sides and can open doors only at the front and back. So the middle rooms are often dark and stuffy. The light well is the classic solution, but if designed wrongly it can become a “chimney” that draws in hot sun, noise and rainwater. This article explains the principles and practical points.
h2
1. How does air move in a townhouse?
p
There are two main mechanisms:
ul

Cross ventilation: air enters through the front door and exits through the rear door (or the reverse). For cross ventilation, the air path must be clear, not blocked by solid walls in the middle of the house.

Stack effect: hot air is lighter, rises and escapes at the top of the light well; cooler air is drawn in through the ground floor doors. The taller the light well and the larger the temperature difference, the stronger the effect.
p
A good light well must have somewhere for hot air to escape at the top. A light well fully covered in glass with no vents will hold heat like a greenhouse.
h2
2. Where to put the light well?
ul
In the middle of the house, beside the stairs: lights both the stairs and the rooms on either side, suited to deep houses.
At the rear of the house (rear light well, rear yard): serves the kitchen, bathroom and drying clothes; easier to waterproof as it is not between rooms.
A very deep house can have two light wells: one in the middle and one at the rear.
p

There is no universal size for a light well; the architect balances it against the house height, the sun direction and the floor area. A light well that is too small for its height hardly brings light down to the ground floor.
h2
3. Covering the light well: closed or open?
ul
Left open with a safety net: best ventilation, but rainwater drainage at the bottom of the well must be handled (sloped floor, drain, careful waterproofing) and you must accept rain blowing in.
Glass roof or fixed skylight: rain-tight, but there must be gaps, flip windows or louvres in the well wall to let hot air out. Use tempered or laminated safety glass and a shading layer.
Opening roof (manual or automatic): flexible but higher in cost and maintenance.
p
Rainwater from the roof and light well must be collected into your own drainage line and not run onto the neighbouring house (Article 250 of the Civil Code).
h2
4. Common mistakes
ol
Fully covering the light well with plastic sheet or ordinary glass with no air vents - the top floor becomes very hot.
Not waterproofing the bottom and walls of the well, so rainwater seeps into the ceiling of the floor below.
A low railing around the light well with large gaps - dangerous for small children.
Using the light well to place air-conditioner outdoor units or pumps - blowing hot air and noise into the house.
Rooms around the light well with no doors opening onto it, so they get light but no breeze.
h2
5. Safety and fire protection
p

A light well and voids let air move well but are also paths for smoke and fire to spread quickly up the floors in a fire. So you need sensible escape routes, a sturdy railing and net, and no flammable items stored at the base of the light well. For fire protection requirements for houses, see Fire prevention and fighting requirements for houses.
h2
6. Complements to the light well
ul
Vent panels and louvres above doors so air still circulates when doors are closed.
Small plants in the rear yard and on the balcony help reduce radiant heat.
Extractor fans to assist bathrooms and kitchens without windows.
p
